Lowpass Filter Design by Pole Placement

An ideal lowpass filter, drawn in blue, passes all frequencies less than ωc and rejects all frequencies greater than ωc. Such a filter cannot be implemented physically because it is non-causal. However, we can design causal filters, drawn in orange, that approximate the ideal lowpass filter. This Demonstration lets you design such a filter by locating poles (of the transfer function), drawn with red ×s, in different arrangements.

Details

Four options are given for filter design by pole placement. All filters are scaled so that the maximum magnitude is about 1.

The first, "vertical line", places n poles equally spaced on the imaginary axis between −j ωc and j ωc, with real component α. The associated magnitude spectrum favors frequencies in the −ωc to ωc range, but the pattern has undesirable resonances at frequencies corresponding to the pole locations along the complex axis.

The second, "triangle", places n poles equally spaced along the imaginary axis between −j ωc and j ωc, with real component α(1 − 0.95 Im(p)), where Im(p) is the imaginary component of the pole. The associated magnitude spectrum again favors frequencies in the −ωc to ωc range, but the pattern has undesirable resonances at −ωc and ωc.

The "Butterworth" filter, introduced in 1930 by British engineer and physicist Stephen Butterworth, places the poles along the circumference of a circle of radius ωc in the left half-plane. The resulting filter is causal, BIBO stable, and flat for low frequencies. The roll-off rate is −20n dB/decade.

Switching to placing poles along an "elliptical" circumference enables faster roll-off, but introduces ripple in the low-frequency range.

Finally, in "manual" mode, you can drag, add, or delete poles and see the resulting effects in the frequency domain.

References
[1] F. Ulaby and A. Yagle, Engineering Signals and Systems, Allendale: NTS Press, 2012.

Browser port of a Wolfram Demonstration. All computation runs in your browser. In "manual" mode, drag a pole on the left plot; Alt-click (⌘-click on a Mac) on empty space adds a pole, on a pole deletes it.
